title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 884–887 (Night 211, continuing nights-210), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 211 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, having heard the disguised Budūr's story, marvels at it, promises to keep the secret, and recites verses on secrets well kept; the two sleep side by side until near dawn, when the princess cuts the throat of a young pigeon over her shift, smears herself with its blood and cries out, so that the household trills for joy, King Armānūs believes the marriage consummated and gives a great feast, and Budūr goes on ruling in the Ebony Islands. The tale then turns back to King Shahramān, who has waited in vain for his son since Qamar al-Zamān rode out to hunt with Marzawān: after a sleepless night he weeps and recites verses, leads out his army, splits it six ways, and at a crossroads finds torn clothes, cut-up flesh and blood, takes them for his son's remains, and mourns him with all his troops in a second poem before returning to his city; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eleventh after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and eleventh night,
sentences.n: al-ḥādiyata ʿashara, “eleventh”: the print has عشر where Classical Arabic would make the second part feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. Compound numbers of this kind keep a fixed -a ending whatever their case. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ السَّيِّدَةَ بُدُورَ لَمَّا أَعْلَمَتْ حَيَاةَ النُّفُوسِ بِقِصَّتِهَا وَأَمَرَتْهَا بِالْكِتْمَانِ فَسَمِعَتْ حَيَاةُ النُّفُوسِ كَلَامَهَا وَتَعَجَّبَتْ مِنْ قِصَّتِهَا غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَرَقَّتْ لَهَا وَدَعَتْ لَهَا بِجَمْعِ شَمْلِهَا عَلَى مَحْبُوبِهَا قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-sayyidata Budūra lammā aʿlamat Ḥayāta al-Nufūsi bi-qiṣṣatihā wa-amarat-hā bi-al-kitmāni fa-samiʿat Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi kalāmahā wa-taʿajjabat min qiṣṣatihā ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-raqqat lahā wa-daʿat lahā bi-jamʿi shamlihā ʿalā maḥbūbihā Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-Lady Budūr, when she-informed Ḥayāt al-Nufūs of-her-story and-commanded-her to-the-keeping-secret, then-heard Ḥayāt al-Nufūs her-speech and-wondered at her-story (the) utmost (of) the-wonder, and-softened to-her, and-prayed for-her for-(the)-gathering (of) her-scattered-state with her-beloved Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the Lady Budūr had told Ḥayāt al-Nufūs her story and bidden her keep it secret, Ḥayāt al-Nufūs listened to her words and marvelled greatly at her story; her heart went out to her, and she prayed that Budūr might be united once more with her beloved Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: The night takes up the last sentence of the one before. Budūra is accusative after anna, with the diptote's -a. aʿlama bi-, Form IV, “to inform of”: bi- marks the thing made known. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes bi- of what is commanded; kitmān, “concealment, keeping a secret”. fa-samiʿat answers lammā with fa-, a loose join common in the storyteller's Arabic. ghāyata al-ʿajabi, “the utmost of wonder”, an accusative of degree. raqqa li-, “to soften towards, feel for”: li- marks the one pitied. daʿā li- … bi-, “to pray for someone for something”: li- marks the one prayed for, bi- the thing asked. jamʿ al-shaml, “the gathering of what was scattered”, the set phrase for reunion; ʿalā, “with”, marks the one she is to be reunited with.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَا أُخْتِي لَا تَخَافِي وَلَا تَفْزَعِي وَاصْبِرِي إِلَى أَنْ يَقْضِيَ اللّٰهُ أَمْرًا كَانَ مَفْعُولًا
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahā yā ukhtī lā takhāfī wa-lā tafzaʿī wa-iṣbirī ilā an yaqḍiya Allāhu amran kāna mafʿūlan
sentences.l: And-she-said to-her: O my-sister, do-not fear and-do-not take-fright, and-be-patient until that God decrees a-matter (that) was done.
sentences.i: And she said to her, “My sister, do not be afraid or alarmed; be patient until God brings about a thing that must come to pass.”
sentences.n: Ḥayāt al-Nufūs now speaks to Budūr as one woman to another: yā ukhtī, “my sister”, with feminine imperatives. faziʿa, “to take fright”. ilā an, “until”, with the subjunctive yaqḍiya. yaqḍiya Allāhu amran kāna mafʿūlan, “until God decides a matter that was to be done”, words of the Qurʾān (8:42, 8:44): what God has decreed is as good as done.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ حَيَاةَ النُّفُوسِ أَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Ḥayāta al-Nufūsi anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: Then indeed Ḥayāt al-Nufūs recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then Ḥayāt al-Nufūs recited:
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, the narrator's way of turning to a new subject: Ḥayāta is accusative after inna. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”: the imperfect describes the reciting.

sentences.t:
اَلسِّرُّ عِنْدِيَ فِيْ بَيْتٍ لَهُ غَلَقُ * قَدْ ضَاعَ مِفْتَاحُهُ وَالْبَيْتُ مَخْتُوْمُ
مَا يَكْتُمُ السِّرَّ اِلَّا كُلُّ ذِيْ ثِقَةٍ * وَالسِّرُّ عِنْدَ خِيَارِ النَّاسِ مَكْتُوْمُ
sentences.tr:
al-sirru ʿindiya fī baytin lahu ghalaqu * qad ḍāʿa miftāḥuhu wa-al-baytu makhtūmu
mā yaktumu al-sirra illā kullu dhī thiqatin * wa-al-sirru ʿinda khiyāri al-nāsi maktūmu
sentences.l:
The-secret with-me (is) in a-house to-which (is) a-lock; * lost-has its-key, and-the-house (is) sealed.
Not keeps the-secret except every one-of trust, * and-the-secret with (the) best (of) the-people (is) hidden.
sentences.i:
A secret with me lies in a house that has a lock; * its key is lost, and the house is sealed.
None keeps a secret but one who is worthy of trust, * and with the best of people a secret stays hidden.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -ūmu, makhtūm, “sealed”, answering maktūm, “hidden”. ʿindiya, “with me”, keeps the old vowel on the -ī of “me” for the metre. ghalaq, “lock, bolt”. ḍāʿa, “to be lost”. dhū thiqatin, “one of trust”, a trustworthy man: dhī is genitive after kullu. khiyār al-nās, “the best of people”. The print sets a bare alif without hamza in اِلَّا, and a sukūn on the long vowel of فِيْ, ذِيْ, مَخْتُوْمُ and مَكْتُوْمُ, as it often does; all are kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا قَالَتْ لَهَا يَا أُخْتِي إِنَّ صُدُورَ الْأَحْرَارِ قُبُورُ الْأَسْرَارِ وَأَنَا لَا أُفْشِي لَكِ سِرًّا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā qālat lahā yā ukhtī inna ṣudūra al-aḥrāri qubūru al-asrāri wa-anā lā ufshī laki sirran
sentences.l: And-when she-finished from her-poetry, she-said to-her: O my-sister, indeed (the) breasts (of) the-free-born (are the) graves (of) the-secrets, and-I, not I-divulge of-yours a-secret.
sentences.i: When she had finished her verses she said to her, “My sister, the breasts of the noble are the graves of secrets; I will not betray any secret of yours.”
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”: min marks what is finished. inna ṣudūra al-aḥrāri qubūru al-asrāri, “the breasts of the free-born are the graves of secrets”, a proverb, rhyming aḥrār / asrār. aḥrār, plural of ḥurr, “free-born”, hence “noble”. afshā, Form IV, “to divulge, spread abroad”; laki, “of yours”: li- marks whose secret it is.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَعِبَتَا وَتَعَانَقَتَا وَتَبَاوَسَتَا وَنَامَتَا إِلَي قَرِيبِ الْأَذَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma laʿibatā wa-taʿānaqatā wa-tabāwasatā wa-nāmatā ilā qarībi al-adhāni
sentences.l: Then they-two-played and-embraced-each-other and-kissed-each-other and-slept until near the-call-to-prayer.
sentences.i: Then the two of them played together, embraced and kissed, and slept until close to the call to the dawn prayer.
sentences.n: The four verbs are dual feminine, -atā, “the two of them (f.)”. taʿānaqa, Form VI, “to embrace one another”; tabāwasa, Form VI, “to kiss one another”, from bawsa, “a kiss”, a word of Persian origin that the later language uses freely. The print writes ilā as الي, with ي for the final alif, as it often does; it is kept. qarīb al-adhān, “near the call to prayer”, here the call to the dawn prayer.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ حَيَاةُ النُّفُوسِ وَأَخَذَتْ فَرْخَ حَمَامٍ وَذَبَحَتْهُ عَلَى قَمِيصِهَا وَتَلَطَّخَتْ بِدَمِهِ وَقَلَعَتْ سِرْوَالَهَا وَصَرَخَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi wa-akhadhat farkha ḥamāmin wa-dhabaḥat-hu ʿalā qamīṣihā wa-talaṭṭakhat bi-damihi wa-qalaʿat sirwālahā wa-ṣarakhat
sentences.l: Then rose Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and-took a-chick (of) pigeon and-slaughtered-it upon her-shift, and-smeared-herself with-its-blood, and-pulled-off her-trousers, and-screamed.
sentences.i: Then Ḥayāt al-Nufūs rose, took a young pigeon and cut its throat over her shift, smeared herself with its blood, pulled off her trousers and cried out.
sentences.n: farkh ḥamām, “a young pigeon”. dhabaḥa, “to slaughter, cut the throat of”. talaṭṭakha bi-, Form V, “to be smeared with”: bi- marks what stains; its shadda is printed. qalaʿa, “to pull off”, of clothes, the later language's usage. sirwāl, “trousers, drawers”, a word from Persian. The blood on the shift is to pass for the blood of the bride's deflowering, and the cry for her pain.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ لَهَا أَهْلُهَا وَزَغْرَتَتِ الْجَوَارِي وَدَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهَا أُمُّهَا وَسَأَلَتْهَا عَنْ حَالِهَا وَدَارَتْ حَوَالَيْهَا وَأَقَامَتْ عِنْدَهَا إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala lahā ahluhā wa-zaghratati al-jawārī wa-dakhalat ʿalayhā ummuhā wa-saʾalat-hā ʿan ḥālihā wa-dārat ḥawālayhā wa-aqāmat ʿindahā ilā al-masāʾi
sentences.l: And-came-in to-her her-family, and-trilled the-slave-girls, and-came-in upon-her her-mother and-asked-her about her-state, and-went-round about-her and-stayed with-her until the-evening.
sentences.i: Her family came in to her, the slave-girls raised their trilling cries of joy, and her mother came in to her, asked how she was, fussed about her, and stayed with her until evening.
sentences.n: dakhala lahā, “came in to her”: li- stands here where Classical has ʿalā, as in the next clause. zaghrata, “to raise the zaghrūṭa”, the women's shrill trilling cry of joy; the print spells it with tāʾ, زغرتت, where the word is more often written with dāl or ṭāʾ; it is kept. jawārī, plural of jāriya, “slave-girl”. dāra ḥawālayhā, “went round about her”, fussed over her. The hamza of سألتها and of المساء is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ فَإِنَّهَا لَمَّا أَصْبَحَتْ قَامَتْ وَذَهَبَتْ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ وَاغْتَسَلَتْ وَصَلَّتِ الصُّبْحَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-malikatu Budūru fa-innahā lammā aṣbaḥat qāmat wa-dhahabat ilā al-ḥammāmi wa-ightasalat wa-ṣallati al-ṣubḥa
sentences.l: And-as-for the-Queen Budūr, indeed-she, when she-was-in-the-morning, rose and-went to the-bath and-washed-herself and-prayed the-dawn.
sentences.i: As for Queen Budūr, when morning came she rose, went to the bath, washed, and prayed the dawn prayer.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-, “as for …”, the narrator's turn to another figure. aṣbaḥa, Form IV, “to be in the morning”. ightasala, Form VIII, “to wash oneself”: the full washing required after intercourse, so the bath keeps up the pretence. ṣallā al-ṣubḥa, “to pray the dawn (prayer)”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَوَجَّهَتْ إِلَى دَارِ الْحُكُومَةِ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّ الْمَمْلَكَةِ وَحَكَمَتْ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: thumma tawajjahat ilā dāri al-ḥukūmati wa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyi al-mamlakati wa-ḥakamat bayna al-nāsi
sentences.l: Then she-turned to (the) house (of) the-judging and-sat on (the) chair (of) the-kingdom and-judged between the-people.
sentences.i: Then she went to the hall of government, sat on the throne of the kingdom, and gave judgement among the people.
sentences.n: tawajjaha ilā, Form V, “to make for”. dār al-ḥukūma, “the house of government”: ḥukūma here is the giving of judgement, and the dār the hall where the ruler hears cases. kursī al-mamlaka, “the chair of the kingdom”, the throne.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ الزَّغَارِيتَ سَأَلَ عَنِ الْخَبَرِ فَأَخْبَرُوهُ بِافْتِضَاضِ بِنْتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Armānūsu al-zaghārīta saʾala ʿani al-khabari fa-akhbarūhu bi-iftiḍāḍi bintihi
sentences.l: And-when heard King Armānūs the-trilling-cries, he-asked about the-news, and-they-told-him of-(the)-deflowering (of) his-daughter.
sentences.i: When King Armānūs heard the cries of joy he asked what had happened, and they told him that his daughter's maidenhead had been taken.
sentences.n: zaghārīt, plural of zaghrūṭa, the trilling cry, spelled with tāʾ as above. akhbara bi-, Form IV, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news. iftiḍāḍ, verbal noun of Form VIII iftaḍḍa, “to deflower”. The hamza of سأل is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ بِذٰلِكَ وَاتَّسَعَ صَدْرُهُ وَانْشَرَحَ وَأَوْلَمَ وَلِيمَةً عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa bi-dhālika wa-ittasaʿa ṣadruhu wa-insharaḥa wa-awlama walīmatan ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: And-he-rejoiced at-that, and-widened his-breast and-was-opened-out, and-he-gave-a-feast a-feast great.
sentences.i: He was glad of it; his heart swelled and was lightened, and he gave a great feast.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause. ittasaʿa ṣadruhu wa-insharaḥa, “his breast widened and opened out”, the Arabic image of gladness: ittasaʿa, Form VIII, and insharaḥa, Form VII. awlama walīmatan, Form IV, “to give a feast”, the verb with its own noun; walīma is above all a wedding feast.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ مُدَّةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati muddatan mina al-zamāni
sentences.l: And-not they-ceased upon that the-state a-span of the-time.
sentences.i: And so things went on for some time.
sentences.n: lam yazālū ʿalā, “they did not cease to be in”, they stayed so. muddatan mina al-zamāni, “a span of time”, an accusative of time.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihimā
sentences.l: This (is) what was of their-(two)-affair.
sentences.i: So much for the two of them.
sentences.n: The narrator's formula for leaving one thread of the story and taking up another. amrihimā, “the affair of the two of them”, dual: Budūr and Ḥayāt al-Nufūs. The print runs mā kāna, “what was”, together as one word, ماكان, here and in the next sentence; it is kept as set.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ فَإِنَّهُ بَعْدَ خُرُوجِ وَلَدِهِ لِلصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ هُوَ وَمَرْزَوَانُ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ صَبَرَ حَتَّى أَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ عَلَيْهِ بَعْدَ خُرُوجِهِمَا فَلَمْ يَجِئْ وَلَدُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-maliki Shahramāna fa-innahu baʿda khurūji waladihi li-al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi huwa wa-Marzawānu kamā taqaddama ṣabara ḥattā aqbala al-laylu ʿalayhi baʿda khurūjihimā fa-lam yajiʾ waladuhu
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) King Shahramān, indeed-he, after (the) going-out (of) his-son for-the-hunting and-the-chase, he and-Marzawān, as went-before, waited until came-on the-night upon-him after their-(two)-going-out, and-not came his-son.
sentences.i: As for King Shahramān: after his son had ridden out to hunt and to chase with Marzawān, as was told before, he waited until night came on, and still his son did not come.
sentences.n: Shahramān, Qamar al-Zamān's father, is genitive with the diptote's -a. li-al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi, “for hunting and the chase”: li- gives the purpose; ṣayd and qanaṣ mean much the same, paired for weight. huwa wa-Marzawānu, “he and Marzawān”: the pronoun huwa is set so that a second name can be joined to the son. kamā taqaddama, “as went before”, the narrator pointing back to an earlier part of the tale. aqbala al-laylu ʿalayhi, “night came on him”. The hamza of يجئ is printed; lam yajiʾ, jussive, “did not come”.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَنَمْ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَطَالَ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ وَقَلِقَ غَايَةَ الْقَلَقِ وَزَادَ وَجْدُهُ وَمَاصَدَّقَ أَنَّ الْفَجْرَ يَطْلُعُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yanam tilka al-laylata wa-ṭāla ʿalayhi al-laylu wa-qaliqa ghāyata al-qalaqi wa-zāda wajduhu wa-mā ṣaddaqa anna al-fajra yaṭluʿu
sentences.l: And-not he-slept that the-night, and-grew-long upon-him the-night, and-he-was-restless (the) utmost (of) the-restlessness, and-increased his-grief, and-not he-believed that the-dawn (would) rise.
sentences.i: He did not sleep that night; the night was long for him, he was beside himself with unrest, his grief grew, and he could hardly wait for the dawn to break.
sentences.n: lam yanam, jussive of nāma, “to sleep”. ṭāla ʿalayhi, “grew long for him”: ʿalā marks the one who bears it. ghāyata al-qalaqi, “the utmost of unrest”, an accusative of degree, as above. wajd, “strong emotion”, here grief and longing. wa-mā ṣaddaqa anna …, “and he could not believe that …”, the spoken language's way of saying that someone could hardly wait for a thing: ṣaddaqa, Form II, “to believe”. The print runs wa-mā ṣaddaqa together as one word, وماصدق; it is kept as set.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ انْتَظَرَ وَلَدَهُ إِلَى نِصْفِ النَّهَارِ فَلَمْ يَجِئْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa intaẓara waladahu ilā niṣfi al-nahāri fa-lam yajiʾ
sentences.l: And-when he-was-in-the-morning, he-awaited his-son until (the) half (of) the-day, and-not he-came.
sentences.i: When morning came he waited for his son until midday, and he did not come.
sentences.n: intaẓara, Form VIII, “to wait for”, takes its object directly. niṣf al-nahār, “the half of the day”, noon. The hamza of يجئ is printed.

sentences.t: فَحَسَّ قَلْبُهُ بِالْفِرَاقِ وَالْتَهَبَ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ بِالْإِشْفَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥassa qalbuhu bi-al-firāqi wa-iltahaba ʿalā waladihi bi-al-ishfāqi
sentences.l: And-sensed his-heart the-parting, and-he-blazed over his-son with-the-anxious-fear.
sentences.i: His heart told him that they were parted, and he burned with fear for his son.
sentences.n: ḥassa bi-, “to sense, feel”, the later language's form of Classical aḥassa bi-: bi- marks what is felt; the shadda of فحسّ is printed. iltahaba, Form VIII, “to blaze up”; ʿalā marks the one he burns for, and bi- what he burns with: ishfāq, Form IV verbal noun, “anxious pity, fear for someone”. The two clauses rhyme, firāq / ishfāq.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ وَاوَلَدَاهْ ثُمَّ بَكَى حَتَّى بَلَّ ثِيَابَهُ بِالدُّمُوعِ وَأَنْشَدَ مِنْ قَلْبٍ مَصْدُوعٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla wā-waladāh thumma bakā ḥattā balla thiyābahu bi-al-dumūʿi wa-anshada min qalbin maṣdūʿin
sentences.l: And-he-said: Alas-my-son! Then he-wept until he-wetted his-clothes with-the-tears, and-recited from a-heart cracked:
sentences.i: “Alas, my son!” he cried; then he wept until his clothes were wet with tears, and from a broken heart he recited:
sentences.n: wā-waladāh, “alas, my son!”, the cry of lament (nudba): wā before the name of the one mourned, the long -ā after it, and a pausal -h; the print sets it as one word, واولداه. balla, “to wet”: bi- marks what wets; the shadda of بلّ is printed. maṣdūʿ, “cracked, split”, of a heart broken with grief. The rhyme falls on dumūʿ / maṣdūʿ.

sentences.t:
مَازِلْتُ مُعْتَرِضًا عَلَى اَهْلِ الْهَوَى * حَتَّى بُلِيْتُ بِحُلْوِهِ وَبِمُرِّهِ
وَشَرِبْتُ كَاسَ صُدُوْدِهِ مُتَجَرِّعًا * وَذَلَلْتُ فِيْهِ لِعَبْدِهِ وَلِحُرِّهِ
نَذَرَ الزَّمَانُ بِاَنْ يُفَرِّقَ شَمْلَنَا * وَالْآنَ قَدْ اَوْفَى الزَّمَانُ بِنَذْرِهِ
sentences.tr:
mā ziltu muʿtariḍan ʿalā ahli al-hawā * ḥattā bulītu bi-ḥulwihi wa-bi-murrihi
wa-sharibtu kāsa ṣudūdihi mutajarriʿan * wa-dhaliltu fīhi li-ʿabdihi wa-li-ḥurrihi
nadhara al-zamānu bi-an yufarriqa shamlanā * wa-al-āna qad awfā al-zamānu bi-nadhrihi
sentences.l:
Not I-ceased objecting against (the) people (of) the-love, * until I-was-tried with-its-sweet and-with-its-bitter.
And-I-drank (the) cup (of) its-aversion, gulping-down, * and-I-was-abased in-it to-its-slave and-to-its-free-man.
Vowed the-time that it-would-scatter our-gathered-state, * and-now has fulfilled the-time its-vow.
sentences.i:
I never ceased to find fault with those who love, * until I was tried with its sweet and with its bitter.
I drank down the cup of its coldness, gulp by gulp, * and in it was brought low before its slave and its free man alike.
Fate vowed that it would scatter all we had together, * and now fate has kept its vow.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and the lines rhyme in -rihi. A love poem, set here in a father's mouth for his lost son. mā ziltu, “I did not cease”, is set as one word (مَازِلْتُ); it is kept as set. iʿtaraḍa ʿalā, Form VIII, “to object to, find fault with”; ahl al-hawā, “the people of love”, lovers. bulītu bi-, passive, “I was tried, afflicted with”: bi- marks the trial. The -hi of ḥulwihi, murrihi, ṣudūdihi, ʿabdihi and ḥurrihi returns to al-hawā, “love”; with ṣudūd, “turning away, coldness”, it may as well be the beloved. kās, “cup”, is printed كَاسَ, without the hamza of kaʾs. tajarraʿa, Form V, “to gulp down a bitter draught”. dhalla li-, “to be abased before”: li- marks the one before whom; love's slave and its free man are all who love and all who do not. nadhara bi-an, “to vow to”: bi- only introduces what is vowed. shaml, “what is gathered together”: to scatter it is to part those who belong together. awfā bi-, Form IV, “to fulfil”: bi- marks what is fulfilled. The print sets a bare alif without hamza in اَهْلِ, بِاَنْ and اَوْفَى, and a sukūn on the long vowel of بُلِيْتُ, صُدُوْدِهِ and فِيْهِ, as it often does; the madda of الْآنَ is printed. All are kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ مَسَحَ دُمُوعَهُ وَنَادَى فِي عَسْكَرِهِ بِالرَّحِيلِ وَالْحَثِّ عَلَى السَّفَرِ الطَّوِيلِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi masaḥa dumūʿahu wa-nādā fī ʿaskarihi bi-al-raḥīli wa-al-ḥaththi ʿalā al-safari al-ṭawīli
sentences.l: And-when he-finished from his-poetry, he-wiped his-tears and-called-out among his-army the-departure and-the-urging to the-journey the-long.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he wiped away his tears and had it proclaimed in his army that they were to break camp and make haste on a long journey.
sentences.n: nādā bi-, Form III, “to proclaim”: bi- marks what is proclaimed; fī, “among”. raḥīl, “setting out, breaking camp”; ḥathth ʿalā, “urging on to”. The rhyme falls on raḥīl / ṭawīl.

sentences.t: فَرَكِبَ الْجَيْشُ جَمِيعُهُ وَخَرَجَ السُّلْطَانُ وَهُوَ مُحْتَرِقُ الْقَلْبِ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَلْبُهُ بِالْحُزْنِ مَلْآنُ
sentences.tr: fa-rakiba al-jayshu jamīʿuhu wa-kharaja al-sulṭānu wa-huwa muḥtariqu al-qalbi ʿalā waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni wa-qalbuhu bi-al-ḥuzni malʾānu
sentences.l: And-mounted the-army, all-of-it, and-went-out the-sultan, and-he (was) burning (of) the-heart over his-son Qamar al-Zamān, and-his-heart with-the-grief (was) full.
sentences.i: The whole army mounted, and the sultan rode out, his heart burning for his son Qamar al-Zamān and filled with grief.
sentences.n: jamīʿuhu, “all of it”, set after the noun it sums up. The king is here called al-sulṭān. wa-huwa …, a clause of state. muḥtariqu al-qalbi, “burnt of heart”: an improper annexation: the participle is narrowed by the part it applies to and stays indefinite. ʿalā, “over, for”, marks the one he grieves for. malʾān bi-, “full of”: bi- marks what fills; the آ of ملآن is printed. The rhyme falls on al-Zamān / malʾān.

sentences.t: وَجَدُّوا فِي سَيْرِهِمْ وَفَرَّقَ الْمَلِكُ جَيْشَهُ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا وَأَمَاماً وَخَلْفاً سِتَّ فِرَقٍ
sentences.tr: wa-jaddū fī sayrihim wa-farraqa al-maliku jayshahu yamīnan wa-shimālan wa-amāman wa-khalfan sitta firaqin
sentences.l: And-they-were-earnest in their-going, and-divided the-king his-army right and-left and-front and-back, six divisions.
sentences.i: They pressed on in earnest, and the king split his army into six bands, to the right and the left, ahead and behind.
sentences.n: jadda fī, “to be earnest in, make haste in”; its shadda is printed, as is that of فرّق. farraqa, Form II, “to divide”; sitta firaqin, “(into) six divisions”, stands as a second accusative. yamīnan wa-shimālan wa-amāman wa-khalfan, accusatives of place. The print sets the tanwīn of amāman and khalfan over the final alif (واماماً وخلفاً); it is kept where printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُمُ الِاجْتِمَاعُ غَدًا عِنْدَ مَفْرِقِ الطَّرِيقِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahumu al-ijtimāʿu ghadan ʿinda mafriqi al-ṭarīqi
sentences.l: And-he-said to-them: The-gathering (is) tomorrow at (the) parting (of) the-road.
sentences.i: And he said to them, “We gather again tomorrow where the road divides.”
sentences.n: al-ijtimāʿu ghadan, “the gathering is tomorrow”, a nominal sentence with the time as its predicate. mafriq al-ṭarīq, “the parting of the road”, a fork or crossroads.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ تَفَرَّقَتِ الْجُيُوشُ وَالْعَسَاكِرُ وَسَافَرُوا وَلَمْ يَزَالُو مُسَافِرِينَ بَقِيَّةَ النَّهَارِ إِلَى أَنْ جَنَّ اللَّيْلُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika tafarraqati al-juyūshu wa-al-ʿasākiru wa-sāfarū wa-lam yazālū musāfirīna baqiyyata al-nahāri ilā an janna al-laylu
sentences.l: And-at that, dispersed the-armies and-the-troops, and-they-journeyed, and-not they-ceased journeying (the) rest (of) the-day until that grew-dark the-night.
sentences.i: At that the armies and troops went their separate ways and set out, and they kept travelling for the rest of the day until night fell.
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “thereupon”. The print writes lam yazālū without the silent alif that Classical spelling sets after the plural -ū (يزالو for يزالوا); it is kept. musāfirīna, accusative as the predicate of zāla. baqiyyata al-nahāri, “the rest of the day”, an accusative of time. janna al-laylu, “night grew dark, came down”.

sentences.t: فَسَارُوا جَمِيعَ اللَّيْلِ إِلَى نِصْفِ النَّهَارِ حَتَّى وَصَلُوا إِلَى مَفْرِقِ أَرْبَعِ طُرُقٍ فَلَمْ يَعْرِفُوا أَيَّ طَرِيقٍ سَلَكَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-sārū jamīʿa al-layli ilā niṣfi al-nahāri ḥattā waṣalū ilā mafriqi arbaʿi ṭuruqin fa-lam yaʿrifū ayya ṭarīqin salakahā
sentences.l: And-they-went all the-night to (the) half (of) the-day, until they-arrived at (the) parting (of) four roads, and-not they-knew which road he-took-it.
sentences.i: They rode all night until noon, till they came to a place where four roads met, and they did not know which road he had taken.
sentences.n: jamīʿa al-layli, “all the night”, an accusative of time. mafriq arbaʿ ṭuruq, “the parting of four roads”, a crossroads. salakahā, “he took it”: the subject is the lost son, and -hā returns to ṭarīq, treated as feminine, as it often is. The shadda of ايّ is printed; ayya is the object of yaʿrifū.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَأَوْا أَثَرَ أَقْمِشَةٍ مُقَطَّعَةٍ وَرَأَوُا اللَّحْمَ مُقَطَّعًا وَنَظَرُوا أَثَرَ الدَّمِ بَاقِيًا وَشَاهَدُوا كُلَّ قِطْعَةٍ مِنَ الثِّيَابِ وَاللَّحْمِ فِي نَاحِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma raʾaw athara aqmishatin muqaṭṭaʿatin wa-raʾawu al-laḥma muqaṭṭaʿan wa-naẓarū athara al-dami bāqiyan wa-shāhadū kulla qiṭʿatin mina al-thiyābi wa-al-laḥmi fī nāḥiyatin
sentences.l: Then they-saw (the) trace (of) cloths cut-to-pieces, and-they-saw the-flesh cut-to-pieces, and-they-saw (the) trace (of) the-blood remaining, and-they-beheld every piece of the-clothes and-the-flesh in a-quarter.
sentences.i: Then they came on shreds of torn cloth, and they saw flesh hacked in pieces and the marks of blood still there, and each scrap of clothing and of flesh lying in a different place.
sentences.n: The print has ونظاروا, a misprint for ونظروا, corrected here. athar, “trace, remains”. aqmisha, plural of qumāsh, “cloth, stuff”. muqaṭṭaʿ, passive participle of Form II qaṭṭaʿa, “cut to pieces”; muqaṭṭaʿan and bāqiyan are accusatives of state. naẓara, “to see”, here takes its object directly, as in the later language. fī nāḥiyatin, “in a quarter”, each in a place of its own. These are the traces laid when Qamar al-Zamān and Marzawān rode off, so that his father would think him dead. The hamza of رأوا and ورأوا is printed; the wāw of raʾaw takes a helping -u before al-.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ ذٰلِكَ صَرَخَ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً مِنْ صَمِيمِ قَلْبِهِ وَقَالَ وَاوَلَدَاهْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-maliku Shahramānu dhālika ṣarakha ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan min ṣamīmi qalbihi wa-qāla wā-waladāh
sentences.l: And-when saw King Shahramān that, he-cried-out a-cry great from (the) core (of) his-heart and-said: Alas-my-son!
sentences.i: When King Shahramān saw this he gave a great cry from the depths of his heart and said, “Alas, my son!”
sentences.n: ṣarakha ṣarkhatan, the verb with its own noun, “cried a great cry”. ṣamīm, “the very core”. wā-waladāh, the cry of lament, as above. The hamza of رأى is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَطَمَ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ وَنَتَفَ لِحْيَتَهُ وَمَزَّقَ أَثْوَابَهُ وَأَيْقَنَ بِمَوْتِ وَلَدِهِ وَزَادَ فِى الْبُكَاءِ وَالنَّحِيبِ
sentences.tr: wa-laṭama ʿalā wajhihi wa-natafa liḥyatahu wa-mazzaqa athwābahu wa-ayqana bi-mawti waladihi wa-zāda fī al-bukāʾi wa-al-naḥībi
sentences.l: And-he-slapped on his-face and-plucked his-beard and-tore his-garments, and-was-certain of-(the)-death (of) his-son, and-increased in the-weeping and-the-sobbing.
sentences.i: He beat his face, tore out his beard and rent his clothes; he was sure that his son was dead, and he wept and sobbed all the more.
sentences.n: laṭama ʿalā wajhihi, “to slap one's face”, a gesture of mourning: the later language puts ʿalā where Classical takes the face directly. natafa, “to pluck out”. mazzaqa, Form II, “to tear to shreds”; its shadda is printed. ayqana bi-, Form IV, “to be certain of”: the verb takes bi- of what one is sure of. zāda fī, “to do more of”. naḥīb, “loud weeping, sobbing”. The print writes fī as فى here; it is kept. The hamza of البكاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَبَكَتْ لِبُكَائِهِ الْعَسَاكِرُ وَكُلُّهُمْ أَيْقَنُوا بِهَلَاكِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَحَثُّوا عَلَى رُؤُسِهِمُ التُّرَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-bakat li-bukāʾihi al-ʿasākiru wa-kulluhum ayqanū bi-halāki Qamari al-Zamāni wa-ḥaththū ʿalā ruʾūsihimu al-turāba
sentences.l: And-wept for-his-weeping the-troops, and-all-of-them were-certain of-(the)-perishing (of) Qamar al-Zamān, and-they-threw upon their-heads the-dust.
sentences.i: The troops wept to see him weep; all of them were sure that Qamar al-Zamān had perished, and they threw dust on their heads.
sentences.n: li-bukāʾihi, “at his weeping”: li- gives the cause; the ئ is printed. bakat … al-ʿasākiru, a feminine singular verb for a broken plural. kulluhum ayqanū, “all of them were certain”, with a plural verb after kulluhum; bi- marks what they were sure of. halāk, “perishing”. Throwing dust on the head is a gesture of mourning. The print sets a shadda on حثّوا, as if from ḥaththa, “to urge”; the phrase belongs to ḥathā, “to scatter, throw (dust)”, which would be ḥathaw. The printed mark is kept and read ḥaththū, but the pointing is doubtful. رؤسهم is printed with ؤ and without the second wāw of ruʾūs, “heads”; the final -u of -himu is a helping vowel before al-.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهِمُ اللَّيْلُ وَهُمْ فِي بُكَاءٍ وَنَحِيبٍ حَتَّى أَشْرَفُوا عَلَى الْهَلَاكِ
sentences.tr: wa-dakhala ʿalayhimu al-laylu wa-hum fī bukāʾin wa-naḥībin ḥattā ashrafū ʿalā al-halāki
sentences.l: And-came-in upon-them the-night while-they (were) in weeping and-sobbing, until they-looked-down upon the-perishing.
sentences.i: Night came down on them as they wept and wailed, until they were close to perishing of it.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalayhim al-laylu, “night came in upon them”. wa-hum fī …, “while they were in …”, a clause of state. ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV, “to look down on”, hence “to be on the brink of”. The hamza of بكاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَاحْتَرَقَ قَلْبُ الْمَلِكِ بِلَهِيبِ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-iḥtaraqa qalbu al-maliki bi-lahībi al-zafarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-burned (the) heart (of) the-king with-(the)-flame (of) the-sighs, and-he-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: The king's heart burned in the flame of his sighs, and he recited these verses:
sentences.n: iḥtaraqa, Form VIII, “to burn, be burnt”; bi- marks what burns it. lahīb, “flame, blaze”; zafarāt, plural of zafra, “a deep sigh, groan”.

sentences.t:
لَاتَعْذُلُوا الْمَحْزُوْنَ فِيْ اَحْزَانِهِ * فَلَقَدْ كَفَاهُ الْوَجْدُ مِنْ اَشْجَانِهِ
يَبْكِيْ لِفَرْطِ تَاَسُّفٍ وَتَوَجُّعٍ * وَغَرَامُهُ يُنْبِيْكَ عَنْ نِيْرَانِهِ
يَا سَعْدُ مَنْ لِمُتَيَّمٍ حَلِفِ الضَّنَى * اَنْ لَايُزِيْلَ الدَّمْعَ مِنْ اَجْفَانِهِ
يُبْدِى الْغَرَامَ لِفَقْدِ بَدْرٍ زَاهِرٍ * بِضِيَائِهِ يَزْهُوْ عَلٰى اَقْرَانِهِ
وَلَقَدْ سَقَاهُ الْمَوْتُ كَاسًا مُتْرَعًا * يَوْمَ الرَّحِيْلِ فَشَطَّ عَنْ اَوْطَانِهِ
تَرَكَ الدِّيَارَ وَسَارَعَنَّا لِلْبَلَا * لَمْ يَحْظُ بِالتَّوْدِيْعِ مِنْ اِخْوَانِهِ
وَلَقَدْ رَمَانِيْ بِالْبِعَادِ وَبِالْجَفَا * وَالصَّدِّ وَالتَّبْرِيْحِ مِنْ هِجْرَانِهِ
وَلَقَدْ مَضَى عَنَّا وَسَارَ مُوَدِّعًا * لَمَّا حَبَاهُ رَبُّهُ بِجَنَانِهِ
sentences.tr:
lā taʿdhulū al-maḥzūna fī aḥzānihi * fa-la-qad kafāhu al-wajdu min ashjānihi
yabkī li-farṭi taʾassufin wa-tawajjuʿin * wa-gharāmuhu yunbīka ʿan nīrānihi
yā Saʿdu man li-mutayyamin ḥalifi al-ḍanā * an lā yuzīla al-damʿa min ajfānihi
yubdī al-gharāma li-faqdi badrin zāhirin * bi-ḍiyāʾihi yazhū ʿalā aqrānihi
wa-la-qad saqāhu al-mawtu kāsan mutraʿan * yawma al-raḥīli fa-shaṭṭa ʿan awṭānihi
taraka al-diyāra wa-sāra ʿannā li-al-balā * lam yaḥẓu bi-al-tawdīʿi min ikhwānihi
wa-la-qad ramānī bi-al-biʿādi wa-bi-al-jafā * wa-al-ṣaddi wa-al-tabrīḥi min hijrānihi
wa-la-qad maḍā ʿannā wa-sāra muwaddiʿan * lammā ḥabāhu rabbuhu bi-janānihi
sentences.l:
Do-not blame the-grieving-one in his-griefs, * for-indeed has-sufficed-him the-passion of his-sorrows.
He-weeps for-(the)-excess (of) regret and-pain, * and-his-love-torment tells-you of its-fires.
O Saʿd, who (is there) for-a-love-enslaved-one, sworn-to the-wasting * that he-will-not remove the-tears from his-eyelids?
He-shows the-love-torment for-(the)-loss (of) a-full-moon shining, * with-its-radiance it-vaunts over its-peers.
And-indeed has-given-him-to-drink the-death a-cup brimming * (on the) day (of) the-departure, and-he-went-far from his-homelands.
He-left the-dwellings and-went from-us to-the-decay; * not he-was-granted the-farewell from his-brothers.
And-indeed he-has-struck-me with-the-distance and-with-the-harshness * and-the-turning-away and-the-torment of his-forsaking.
And-indeed he-has-passed from-us and-gone bidding-farewell, * when favoured-him his-Lord with-His-gardens.
sentences.i:
Do not blame the grieving man for his griefs: * his passion is enough for him, of all his sorrows.
He weeps for the depth of his regret and pain, * and his love will tell you of the fires within.
O Saʿd, who will help a love-slave, sworn to wasting, * sworn never to wipe the tears from his eyelids?
He shows his love-pain for the loss of a shining full moon * that outshone its peers in its radiance.
Death has given him a brimming cup to drink * on the day of parting, and he has gone far from his homeland.
He left his home and went from us to decay, * and had no leave-taking from his brothers.
He has struck me with distance and with harshness, * with coldness and the torment of his leaving.
He has passed from us and gone with a farewell, * since his Lord has granted him His gardens.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and every line rhymes in -ānihi. A lament in the manner of a love poem: the lost son is a shining full moon, badr, and the grieving father speaks of himself as “he”. lā taʿdhulū, “do not blame”, and an lā yuzīla are each set as one word (لَاتَعْذُلُوا, لَايُزِيْلَ); wa-sāra ʿannā, “and went from us”, is set as one word too (وَسَارَعَنَّا): it is not sāraʿa, “to hasten”, for the shadda on the nūn marks ʿannā. All are kept as set. ʿadhala fī, “to blame for”. kafāhu, “has been enough for him”: his own passion is burden enough without blame; min marks what it is made of. li-farṭi, “for excess of”: li- gives the cause; taʾassuf, Form V, “grief, regret”. yunbīka ʿan, “tells you of”, for Classical yunbiʾuka, the hamza given up. Yā Saʿdu, “O Saʿd”, the companion the poets conventionally address. man li-mutayyamin, “who is there for a love-slave?”, who will help him: li- marks the one in need; mutayyam, “enslaved by love”. ḥalif al-ḍanā, “sworn to wasting”: the print points ḥalif, where ḥalīf, “bound by oath, ally”, is the usual form; an lā yuzīla …, “that he will not remove …”, is what he is sworn to. abdā, Form IV, “to show openly”. zahā ʿalā, “to vaunt over, outshine”: bi-ḍiyāʾihi, “by its radiance”: bi- marks the means; aqrān, “peers”. kās, “cup”, for kaʾs, and mutraʿ, “brimming”. shaṭṭa ʿan, “to go far from”. li-al-balā, “to decay”: li- marks where he went; balā is balāʾ without its hamza. lam yaḥẓu bi-, “he was not granted”: bi- marks what is granted; the print points yaḥẓu, where the Classical jussive of ḥaẓiya is yaḥẓa; it is kept as printed. ramā bi-, “to strike with”: bi- marks the missile; jafā, “harshness”, for jafāʾ; tabrīḥ, Form II, “torment”; hijrān, “forsaking”. ḥabā bi-, “to favour with”: bi- marks the gift. bi-janānihi: the print points janān, “heart”, where the sense seems to want jinān, “gardens”, that is, Paradise; it is kept as printed and translated by the sense, but the reading is doubtful. The print writes a bare alif without hamza in اَحْزَانِهِ, اَشْجَانِهِ, تَاَسُّفٍ, اَنْ, اَجْفَانِهِ, اَقْرَانِهِ, اَوْطَانِهِ and اِخْوَانِهِ, yubdī as يُبْدِى, a dagger alif in عَلٰى, and a sukūn on many long vowels (فِيْ, يَبْكِيْ, نِيْرَانِهِ); all are kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ مِنْ إِنْشَادِهِ رَجَعَ بِجُيُوشِهِ إِلَى مَدِينَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha al-maliku Shahramānu min inshādihi rajaʿa bi-juyūshihi ilā madīnatihi
sentences.l: And-when finished King Shahramān from his-reciting, he-returned with-his-armies to his-city.
sentences.i: When King Shahramān had finished reciting, he went back with his armies to his city.
sentences.n: rajaʿa bi-, “to go back with”: bi- marks those he takes along.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد; they are kept as set.
